{{Short description|Shared independent set of two matroids}}
In [[combinatorial optimization]], the '''matroid intersection''' problem is to find a largest common independent set in two [[matroid]]s over the same ground set. If the elements of the matroid are assigned real weights, the '''weighted matroid intersection''' problem is to find a common independent set with the maximum possible weight. These problems generalize many problems in graph theory and combinatorial optimization including finding [[maximum matching]]s and [[maximum weight matching]]s in [[bipartite graph]]s and finding [[Arborescence (graph theory)|arborescence]]s in [[directed graph]]s.

The '''matroid intersection theorem''', due to [[Jack Edmonds]],<ref name=":0">{{citation
 | last = Edmonds
 | first = Jack
 | contribution = Submodular functions, matroids, and certain polyhedra
 | editor = R. Guy |editor2=H. Hanam |editor3=N. Sauer |editor4=J. Schonheim
 | title = Combinatorial structures and their applications (Proc. 1969 Calgary Conference)
 | pages = 69&ndash;87
 | publisher = Gordon and Breach, New York
 | year = 1970
}}. Reprinted in M. Jünger et al. (Eds.): Combinatorial Optimization (Edmonds Festschrift), LNCS 2570, pp. 1126, Springer-Verlag, 2003.</ref> 
says that for any two matroids <math>M_1 = (E, \mathcal I_1)</math> and <math>M_2 = (E, \mathcal I_2)</math> we have
:<math>\max_{I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2} |I| = \min_{A\subseteq E}(r_1(A)+r_2(E\setminus A))</math>
where <math>r_1</math> and <math>r_2</math> are the respective rank functions of <math>M_1</math> and <math>M_2</math>. In other words, there is always a simple upper bound proof, consisting of a partitioning of the ground set amongst the two matroids, whose value (the sum of the respective [[Matroid rank|ranks]]) equals the size of a maximum common independent set.

Based on this theorem, the matroid intersection problem for two matroids can be solved in polynomial time using [[matroid partitioning]] algorithms.

==Examples==
Let ''G''&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''U'',''V'';''E'') be a [[bipartite graph]]. One may define a [[partition matroid]] ''M<sub>U</sub>'' on the ground set ''E'', in which a set of edges is independent if no two of the edges have the same endpoint in ''U''. Similarly one may define a matroid ''M<sub>V</sub>'' in which a set of edges is independent if no two of the edges have the same endpoint in ''V''. Any set of edges that is independent in both ''M<sub>U</sub>'' and ''M<sub>V</sub>'' has the property that no two of its edges share an endpoint; that is, it is a [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]]. Thus, the largest common independent set of ''M<sub>U</sub>'' and ''M<sub>V</sub>'' is a [[maximum matching]] in ''G''.

Similarly, if each edge has a weight, then the maximum-weight independent set of ''M<sub>U</sub>'' and ''M<sub>V</sub>'' is a [[Maximum weight matching]] in ''G''.

== Algorithms ==
There are several polynomial-time algorithms for weighted matroid intersection, with different run-times. The run-times are given in terms of  <math>n</math> - the number of elements in the common base-set, <math>r</math> - the maximum between the ranks of the two matroids,  <math>T</math> - the number of operations required for a [[circuit-finding oracle]], and <math>k</math> - the number of elements in the intersection (in case we want to find an intersection of a specific size <math>k</math>).

* [[Jack Edmonds|Edmonds]]' algorithm uses [[linear programming]] and polyhedra.<ref name=":0" />
* [[Eugene Lawler|Lawler]]'s algorithm.<ref>{{citation |last=Lawler |first=Eugene L. |title=Matroid intersection algorithms |journal=Mathematical Programming |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=31–56 |year=1975 |doi=10.1007/BF01681329 |author-link=Eugene Lawler |s2cid=206801650}}</ref> 
* Iri and Tomizawa's algorithm<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Iri |first1=Masao |last2=Tomizawa |first2=Nobuaki |date=1976 |title=An Algorithm for Finding an Optimal "Independent Assignment" |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jorsj/19/1/19_KJ00001202068/_article/-char/ja/ |journal=日本オペレーションズ・リサーチ学会論文誌 |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=32–57 |doi=10.15807/jorsj.19.32|doi-access=free }}</ref> 
* [[András Frank|Andras Frank]]'s algorithm<ref>{{citation |last=Frank |first=András |title=A weighted matroid intersection algorithm |journal=Journal of Algorithms |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=328–336 |year=1981 |doi=10.1016/0196-6774(81)90032-8}}</ref> uses <math>O(n ^3 T)</math> arithmetic operations.
* [[James B. Orlin|Orlin]] and Vande-Vate's algorithm.<ref>{{Cite report |last1=Orlin |first1=James B. |last2=VandeVate |first2=John|type=Sloan School of Management Working Paper #1446-83 |date=1983 |title=On a "primal" matroid intersection algorithm |hdl=1721.1/2050}}</ref>
* Cunningham's algorithm<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cunningham |first=William H. |date=1986-11-01 |title=Improved Bounds for Matroid Partition and Intersection Algorithms |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0215066 |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |language=en |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=948–957 |doi=10.1137/0215066 |issn=0097-5397|url-access=subscription }}</ref> requires <math>O(r^{1.5}n T)</math> operations on general matroids, and <math>O(n r^{2} \log{r})</math> operations on [[linear matroid]], for two ''r''-by-''n'' matrices.
* Brezovec, Cornuejos and Glover<ref name=":1">{{citation |last1=Brezovec |first1=Carl |title=Two algorithms for weighted matroid intersection |journal=Mathematical Programming |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=39–53 |year=1986 |doi=10.1007/BF02591988 |last2=Cornuéjols |first2=Gérard |last3=Glover |first3=Fred |author2-link=Gérard Cornuéjols |s2cid=34567631}}</ref> present two algorithms for weighted matroid intersection. 
** The first algorithm requires that all weights be integers, and finds an intersection of cardinality <math>k</math> in time <math>O((n^3 k^2 + n k T)\cdot(1+\log{W}))</math>.
** The second algorithm runs in time <math>O(n r \cdot (\log{n}+r+T))</math>.
* Huang, Kakimura and Kamiyama<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Chien-Chung |last2=Kakimura |first2=Naonori |last3=Kamiyama |first3=Naoyuki |date=2019-09-01 |title=Exact and approximation algorithms for weighted matroid intersection |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10107-018-1260-x |journal=Mathematical Programming |language=en |volume=177 |issue=1 |pages=85–112 |doi=10.1007/s10107-018-1260-x |issn=1436-4646|hdl=2324/1474903 |s2cid=254138118 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> show that the weighted matroid intersection problem can be solved by solving ''W'' instances of the unweighted matroid intersection problem, where ''W'' is the largest given weight, assuming that all given weights are integral. This algorithm is faster than previous algorithms when ''W'' is small. They also present an [[approximation algorithm]] that finds an ''e''-approximate solution by solving <math>O(\epsilon^{-1}\log {r})</math> instances of the unweighted matroid intersection problem, where ''r'' is the smaller rank of the two input matroids.
* Ghosh, Gurjar and Raj<ref>{{Citation |last1=Ghosh |first1=Sumanta |chapter=A Deterministic Parallel Reduction from Weighted Matroid Intersection Search to Decision |date=2022-01-01 |chapter-url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/1.9781611977073.44 |title=Proceedings of the 2022 Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) |pages=1013–1035 |series=Proceedings |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |doi=10.1137/1.9781611977073.44 |access-date=2022-11-28 |last2=Gurjar |first2=Rohit |last3=Raj |first3=Roshan|isbn=978-1-61197-707-3 |s2cid=245799113 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> study the run-time complexity of matroid intersection in the [[parallel computing]] model.
* Bérczi, Király, Yamaguchi and Yokoi<ref>{{Cite arXiv|last1=Bérczi |first1=Kristóf |last2=Király |first2=Tamás |last3=Yamaguchi |first3=Yutaro |last4=Yokoi |first4=Yu |date=2022-09-28 |title=Matroid Intersection under Restricted Oracles |class=cs.DS |eprint=2209.14516 }}</ref> present strongly polynomial-time algorithms for weighted matroid intersection using more restricted oracles.

==Extensions==

=== Maximizing weight subject to cardinality ===
In a variant of weighted matroid intersection, called "(P<sub>k</sub>)", the goal is to find a common independent set with the maximum possible weight among all such sets with cardinality ''k'', if such a set exists. This variant, too, can be solved in polynomial time.<ref name=":1" />

=== Three matroids ===
The matroid intersection problem becomes [[NP-hard]] when three matroids are involved, instead of only two.

One proof of this hardness result uses a [[Reduction (complexity)|reduction]] from the [[Hamiltonian path]] problem in [[directed graph]]s. Given a directed graph ''G'' with ''n'' vertices, and specified nodes ''s'' and ''t'', the Hamiltonian path problem is the problem of determining whether there exists a simple path of length ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 that starts at ''s'' and ends at ''t''. It may be assumed without loss of generality that ''s'' has no incoming edges and ''t'' has no outgoing edges. Then, a Hamiltonian path exists if and only if there is a set of ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 elements in the intersection of three matroids on the edge set of the graph: two partition matroids ensuring that the in-degree and out-degree of the selected edge set are both at most one, and the [[graphic matroid]] of the [[undirected graph]] formed by forgetting the edge orientations in ''G'', ensuring that the selected edge set has no cycles.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Welsh | first = D. J. A. | author-link = Dominic Welsh
 | isbn = 9780486474397
 | page = 131
 | publisher = Courier Dover Publications
 | title = Matroid Theory
 | year = 2010 | orig-year = 1976}}.
</ref>

=== Matroid parity ===
Another computational problem on matroids, the [[matroid parity problem]], was formulated by Lawler<ref>{{citation
 | last = Lawler | first = Eugene L. | author-link = Eugene Lawler
 | contribution = Chapter 9: The Matroid Parity Problem
 | contribution-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=MTuoAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA356
 | location = New York
 | mr = 0439106
 | pages = 356–367
 | publisher = Holt, Rinehart and Winston
 | title = Combinatorial Optimization: Networks and Matroids
 | year = 1976}}.</ref> as a common generalization of matroid intersection and non-bipartite graph matching. However, although it can be solved in polynomial time for [[linear matroid]]s, it is NP-hard for other matroids, and requires exponential time in the [[matroid oracle]] model.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Jensen | first1 = Per M.
 | last2 = Korte | first2 = Bernhard | author2-link = Bernhard Korte
 | doi = 10.1137/0211014
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Computing]]
 | mr = 646772
 | pages = 184–190
 | title = Complexity of matroid property algorithms
 | volume = 11
 | year = 1982}}.</ref>

=== Valuated matroids ===
A '''valuated matroid''' is a matroid equipped with a value function ''v'' on the set of its bases, with the following ''exchange property'': for any two distinct bases <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, if <math>a\in A\setminus B</math>, then there exists an element <math>b\in B\setminus A</math> such that both <math>(A \setminus \{ a \}) \cup \{b\}</math> and <math>(B \setminus \{ b \}) \cup \{a\}</math> are bases, and :<math>v(A)+v(B) \leq v(B \setminus \{ b \} \cup \{a\}) + v(A \setminus \{ a \} \cup \{b\})</math>.

Given a weighted [[bipartite graph]] ''G'' = (''X''+''Y'', ''E'') and two valuated matroids, one on ''X'' with bases set ''B<sub>X</sub>'' and valuation ''v<sub>X</sub>'', and one on ''Y'' with bases ''B<sub>Y</sub>'' and valuation ''v<sub>Y</sub>'', the '''valuated independent assignment problem''' is the problem of finding a matching  ''M'' in ''G'', such that ''M<sub>X</sub>'' (the subset of ''X'' matched by ''M'') is a base in ''B<sub>X</sub>'', ''M<sub>Y</sub>'' is a base in ''B<sub>Y</sub>'', and subject to this, the sum <math>w(M) + v_X(M_X)+v_Y(M_Y)</math> is maximized. The weighted matroid intersection problem is a special case in which the matroid valuations are constant, so we only seek to maximize <math>w(M)</math> subject to ''M<sub>X</sub>'' is a base in ''B<sub>X</sub>'' and ''M<sub>Y</sub>'' is a base in ''B<sub>Y</sub>'' ''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Murota |first=Kazuo |date=1996-11-01 |title=Valuated Matroid Intersection I: Optimality Criteria |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/S0895480195279994 |journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=545–561 |doi=10.1137/S0895480195279994 |issn=0895-4801|url-access=subscription }}</ref>'' Murota presents a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Murota |first=Kazuo |date=November 1996 |title=Valuated Matroid Intersection II: Algorithms |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/S0895480195280009 |journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics |language=en |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=562–576 |doi=10.1137/S0895480195280009 |issn=0895-4801|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
